rows.verified: HSE identifies slips and trips as a major and widely preventable cause of workplace injury.
Employers must assess slip and trip risks and take reasonably practicable action to control them.
Workplace floors must be suitable, in good condition and free from obstructions so people can move safely.
Floor contamination, surface condition, footwear, cleaning and human factors all influence slip risk.
Cleaning can itself create hazards through damp floors, trailing cables and poorly controlled access.
Risk assessment should consider wet and dry contamination, obstructions, uneven surfaces, changes of level, lighting and handrails.
Workers should report hazards and near misses, clear spillages promptly and keep walkways free from obstacles.
HSE states that many slip and trip controls are simple and low cost when hazards are identified early.
Slip and trip risk depends on flooring, contamination, cleaning, footwear, lighting, route design, behaviour and maintenance.
HSE slip evidence is workplace-, route-, surface-, task-, person- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level injury probability.
Work at height is work where a person could fall a distance liable to cause personal injury if precautions were absent.
The Work at Height Regulations 2005 apply to employers and others who control work-at-height activities.
Work must be properly planned, supervised and carried out by competent people using suitable equipment.
Dutyholders should first avoid work at height where reasonably practicable, for example by doing work from ground level.
Where height work cannot be avoided, collective fall-prevention measures should be considered before measures that only minimise consequences.
Risks from fragile surfaces must be assessed and properly managed.
Equipment used for work at height must be selected appropriately, inspected and maintained.
Work at height includes falls from edges, through openings or fragile surfaces, and into floor openings or holes.
Fall risk depends on task, height, surface, edge protection, access equipment, weather, supervision and worker competence.
HSE height evidence is task-, location-, equipment-, worker-, condition- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level fall probability.
